trial_name: ELAD — Extracorporeal Cellular Therapy in Severe Alcoholic Hepatitis (2018)
citation: Thompson J, Jones N, Al-Khafaji A, Malik S, Reich D, Munoz S, et al. Extracorporeal cellular therapy (ELAD) in severe alcoholic hepatitis: a multinational, prospective, controlled, randomised trial. Liver Transpl. 2018;24(3):380-393
one_liner: In severe alcoholic hepatitis, ELAD did not improve overall survival compared with standard of care (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.69–1.53, P=0.90).

pico.population: Hospitalised adults with severe alcoholic hepatitis (bilirubin ≥8 mg/dL, Maddrey’s DF ≥32, MELD 18–35)
pico.intervention: Continuous ELAD therapy for up to 120 hours (3–5 days) plus standard of care
pico.comparison: Standard of care alone (guideline-based management, no sham device)

background.existing_knowledge: Severe alcoholic hepatitis has high short-term mortality despite supportive care. Pharmacotherapy (corticosteroids, pentoxifylline) has limited, inconsistent survival benefit and contraindications. Early liver transplantation can improve outcomes in selected non-responders but is limited by eligibility and organ availability.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether bioartificial liver support with ELAD can improve survival in sAH beyond standard care.
background.hypothesis: Adding 3–5 days of continuous ELAD therapy to guideline-based standard of care improves overall survival compared with standard of care alone.

methods.design: Multinational, prospective, multicentre (40 sites), randomised (1:1), open-label, stratified (Stratum A vs B), parallel-group, controlled superiority trial.
methods.setting: 40 sites in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia; hospitalised patients managed in specialist inpatient services.

inclusion: Clinical sAH with jaundice (bilirubin ≥8 mg/dL) and coagulopathy (Maddrey’s DF ≥32)
Stratum A: biopsy-proven sAH or ≥2 of hepatomegaly, AST>ALT, leukocytosis, ascites; Stratum B: sAH with underlying chronic liver disease not due to alcohol
exclusion: End-stage cirrhosis features (liver size <10 cm, liver volume <750 cc, or portal vein thrombosis)
Significant concomitant disease with life expectancy <3 months

methods.intervention: ELAD + standard of care: blood drawn via dual-lumen catheter, ultrafiltrate separated and circulated through 4 hollow-fibre cartridges containing ~440 g C3A cells, then filtered (0.2 µm) and returned. Continuous therapy for up to 120 hours (3–5 days); could stop after 72 hours if rapid response. Anticoagulation per site protocols for continuous haemofiltration, no citrate.
methods.comparison: Standard of care alone: AASLD/EASL guideline-based management for complications of liver disease; concomitant sAH medications (corticosteroids, pentoxifylline, N-acetylcysteine, antibiotics) permitted. No sham device.
methods.blinding: Open-label; primary endpoint (mortality) is objective, but non-fatal outcomes susceptible to bias. Follow-up health assessments by independent physician/nurse practitioner.
methods.sample_size_power: 200 subjects (100 per group) to detect a 20% absolute increase in 91-day survival (from 40% to 60%) with ≥95% power at 5% significance level using log-rank test.
methods.follow_up: Minimum 91 days after randomisation of last subject; scheduled assessments daily for week 1, then days 7, 14, 21, 28, 63, 91; extension protocol collected survival up to 5 years.

headline_bullets: ELAD did not improve overall survival: HR 1.03 (95% CI 0.69–1.53, P=0.90).
Biochemical response was greater with ELAD (bilirubin reduction >20% by day 7: 59% vs 23%; Lille responders 74.7% vs 47%), but this did not translate to survival benefit.
Prespecified subgroup trends suggested possible benefit in younger/lower-MELD patients and harm in older/higher-MELD patients.

outcomes_table.note: Secondary endpoint; between-group comparison not reported
Secondary endpoint; between-group comparison not reported
Higher early response did not translate to survival benefit

subgroup_table.note: n=120; trend towards lower mortality with ELAD
n=101; trend towards lower mortality with ELAD

subgroup_table.subgroup: Post-hoc combined: MELD <28 and age <46.9 years (day-91 survival)

safety: Two deaths judged related to ELAD: DIC precipitation (baseline MELD >28) and catheter insertion complication.
TEAEs of interest (ELAD vs SOC): anaemia 44% vs 16%, thrombocytopenia 35% vs 11%, coagulopathy 31% vs 12%, hypotension 31% vs 17%.
Nonserious adverse events increased with ELAD, predominantly haematological and haemodynamic.

domains.notes: Block randomisation (block size 4) with 1:1 allocation; stratified schedules for Stratum A and B; allocation concealment via computerised eCRF and sponsor hotline code assignment. Uneven group sizes (96 vs 107) due to incomplete blocks.

Open-label design without sham extracorporeal support increases risk of differential co-interventions and reporting of non-fatal outcomes. Primary endpoint (mortality) is objective and less susceptible to adjudication bias.

At 91 days: 1 lost to follow-up in each arm; 2 withdrew consent in control arm; outcome known in 95 ELAD vs 104 control. Extension follow-up: outcome known in 94 ELAD vs 102 control; 1 ELAD and 3 control lost; 1 ELAD and 2 control withdrew consent. ITT used for efficacy.

Only 45/96 (46.9%) completed 120 hours of ELAD; 37 completed 72–120 hours; 12 received <72 hours; 2 did not initiate. Discontinuations often due to adverse events (n=18) or investigator judgement of instability (n=9). One control subject inadvertently received ELAD (as-treated: 95 ELAD, 108 control).

Mean MELD 27.3; mean bilirubin 25.1 mg/dL; vasopressors in 38 subjects evenly distributed. Ventilator support: 8 ELAD vs 3 control; acute dialysis: 2 ELAD vs 0 control. Control arm had higher proportion aged <35 years. Time between last alcohol intake, hospitalisation, and randomisation comparable.
Prednisone standard dose: 34.4% ELAD vs 42.1% control; systemic antibiotics: 60.4% vs 54.2%; pentoxifylline: 34.4% vs 31.8%.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate internal validity: randomisation with allocation concealment and objective mortality endpoint are strengths, but open-label design and substantial truncation/non-initiation of ELAD exposure limit separation and complicate causal attribution.

domains.notes: Participants reflect hospitalised sAH with very high bilirubin (mean 25.1 mg/dL) and MELD 18–35 (mean 27.3) across multiple countries. Exclusions (MELD >35, chronic dialysis, severe thrombocytopenia, haemodynamic instability, uncontrolled infection, end-stage cirrhosis, rapidly improving bilirubin) limit generalisability. Inability to provide informed consent was a common screening failure (39/171 exclusions), potentially selecting against more encephalopathic or unstable ICU patients.

ELAD requires specialised equipment, trained staff, continuous extracorporeal circuit management, and reliable vascular access, limiting feasibility to high-resource settings. Does not provide toxin removal or renal support, limiting applicability in multi-organ failure. Enrolled some high-acuity features (vasopressors, ventilation, dialysis) but many ICU extremes excluded.

external_validity.verdict: Limited-to-moderate generalisability: most applicable to hospitalised sAH patients meeting trial’s physiological and imaging constraints in specialised centres; less applicable to sickest ICU cohorts with profound coagulopathy, uncontrolled infection, or established renal failure.

strengths: Large contemporary multicentre, multinational RCT of a complex device intervention in sAH.
Objective primary endpoint (mortality) with minimum 91-day follow-up and pre-planned extension for longer-term survival.
Detailed reporting of treatment exposure, discontinuation reasons, and safety signals specific to extracorporeal therapies.
Demonstrated mechanistic/biological separation (bilirubin reduction, Lille response, IL1Ra signal) enabling refined hypothesis generation.
limitations: Open-label design without sham procedure introduces risk of differential management and subjective outcome reporting.
Substantial non-completion of intended 120-hour ELAD dose (only 45/96 completed), with discontinuations often related to adverse events/instability.
Selection constraints (consent capacity, exclusion of rapidly improving bilirubin and end-stage cirrhosis) may limit applicability to broader ICU sAH population.
Safety profile includes increased haematological and haemodynamic adverse events and two deaths judged related to ELAD.

critical_appraisal.summary: ELAD is a well-conducted but open-label RCT that failed to show survival benefit despite clear biochemical signals; incomplete treatment exposure and procedure-related harms undermine confidence in any potential benefit, and the trial highlights the importance of patient selection for extracorporeal liver support.
weaknesses: Limited generalisability to sickest ICU patients

sections.authors_conclusion: ELAD did not improve survival in an unselected sAH population meeting trial criteria, and its adverse event profile was non-trivial; routine clinical use is not supported by this trial.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: ELAD does not change practice; it should not be used outside clinical trials.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hospitalised patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis meeting trial inclusion criteria (MELD 18–35, no end-stage cirrhosis, no uncontrolled infection or haemodynamic instability).
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That extracorporeal liver support is futile in all patients; subgroup signals suggest possible benefit in younger, lower-MELD patients, but this is hypothesis-generating only.
implementation_caveats: ELAD is not commercially available; this trial informs future device development.
Clinicians should focus on optimal supportive care, complication management, and selective corticosteroid use per guidelines.

controversies.topic: Neutral primary endpoint despite biochemical signals
controversies.notes: Contemporaneous editorial critique emphasised that improved early surrogate signals (bilirubin dynamics; Lille response) did not translate into improved 91-day survival, limiting the clinical case for ELAD as implemented.

controversies.topic: Subgroup signal versus multiplicity and mechanistic plausibility
controversies.notes: The editorial highlighted opposing directional trends across prespecified median-split subgroups (suggested benefit in younger/lower MELD; worse outcomes in older/higher MELD), raising the possibility that extracorporeal therapy harms can offset benefit as physiological reserve decreases.

controversies.topic: Broader extracorporeal liver support evidence base
controversies.notes: A systematic review/meta-analysis of artificial and bioartificial liver support systems in acute liver failure populations reported heterogeneous trials with uncertain survival benefit, reinforcing that extracorporeal liver support remains investigational and highly context-dependent.

Modern guidance for alcohol-associated liver disease prioritises optimal supportive care, complication management, infection evaluation, and selective corticosteroid use; it does not recommend bioartificial liver support devices outside clinical trials.

unresolved_questions: Could a longer duration of ELAD or different patient selection (younger, lower MELD) yield survival benefit?
What is the optimal balance between biochemical efficacy and procedure-related harm in extracorporeal liver support?
Can biomarkers identify patients who might benefit from bioartificial liver support?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: ELAD did not improve survival in severe alcoholic hepatitis and should not be used outside trials; biochemical improvements did not translate to patient benefit.
